In mathematics, '''Wiener's lemma''' is a well-known identity which relates the asymptotic behaviour of the Fourier coefficients of a [[Borel measure]] on the [[Circle group|circle]] to its discrete part. This result admits an analogous statement for measures on the [[real line]]. It was first discovered by [[Norbert Wiener]].<ref>{{citation|url=https://mathoverflow.net/questions/44234/furstenbergs-conjecture-on-2-3-invariant-continuous-probability-measures-on-the|title=Furstenberg's Conjecture on 2-3-invariant continuous probability measures on the circle (MathOverflow)}}</ref><ref>{{citation|url=https://mathoverflow.net/questions/64173/a-complex-borel-measure-whose-fourier-transform-goes-to-zero|title=A complex borel measure, whose Fourier transform goes to zero (MathOverflow)}}</ref>

==Definition==
Consider the space <math>M(\mathbb{T})</math> of all (finite) complex Borel measures on the [[Circle group|unit circle]] <math>\mathbb T</math> and the space <math>C(\mathbb{T})</math> of [[continuous functions]] on <math>\mathbb T</math> as its [[dual space]]. Then <math>C(\mathbb{T}) \sub L^p(\mathbb{T})</math> for all <math>1 \leq p < \infty</math> and <math> L^1(\mathbb{T}) \sub M(\mathbb{T})</math>.{{sfn|Helson|2010|pp=15,19}}

Given <math>\mu \in M(\mathbb{T})</math>, let
<math display="block">\mu_{pp}=\sum_j c_j\delta_{z_j},</math>
be its [[Discrete_measure|discrete]] part (meaning that <math>\mu(\{z_j\})=c_j\neq 0</math> and <math>\mu(\{z\})=0</math> for <math>z\not\in\{z_j\}</math>. Then
<math display="block">\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{1}{2N+1}\sum_{n=-N}^N|\widehat\mu(n)|^2=\sum_j|c_j|^2,</math>
where <math>\widehat{\mu}(n)=\int_{\mathbb T}z^{-n}\,d\mu(z)</math> is the <math>n</math>-th [[Fourier_series#Fourier-Stieltjes_series|Fourier-Stieltjes coefficient]] of <math>\mu</math>.{{sfn|Katznelson|1976|p=45}}{{sfn|Helson|2010|pp=22-24}}

Similarly, on the [[real line]] <math>\mathbb R</math>, the space <math>M(\mathbb{R})</math> is the dual space of <math>C_{0}(\mathbb{R})</math>, [[Function_space#Functional_analysis|continuous functions which vanish at infinity]], and <math>C_{0}(\mathbb{R})\subset L^p(\mathbb{R})</math> for all <math>1 \leq p \leq \infty</math>.{{sfn|Katznelson|1976|p=144}}

Given <math>\mu \in M(\mathbb{R})</math>, let 
<math display="block">\mu_{pp}=\sum_j c_j\delta_{x_j},</math>
its discrete part. Then
<math display="block">\lim_{R\to\infty}\frac{1}{2R}\int_{-R}^R|\widehat\mu(\xi)|^2\,d\xi=\sum_j|c_j|^2,</math>
where <math>\widehat{\mu}(\xi)=\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-2\pi i\xi x}\,d\mu(x)</math> is the [[Fourier_transform#Fourier–Stieltjes_transform_on_measurable_spaces|Fourier-Stieltjes transform]] of <math>\mu</math>.{{sfn|Katznelson|1976|pp=153-154}}

===Consequences===
If <math>\mu \in M(\mathbb{T})</math> is continuous, then 
<math display="block">\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{1}{2N+1}\sum_{n=-N}^N|\widehat\mu(n)|^2=0.</math>
Furthermore, <math>\hat{\mu}</math> tends to zero if <math>\mu</math> is [[Absolute_continuity#Absolutely_continuous_measure|absolutely continuous]].{{sfn|Helson|2010|p=24}} Equivalently, <math>\mu</math> is absolutely continuous if its Fourier-Stieltjes sequence belongs to the [[Sequence_space#ℓp_spaces|sequence space <math>\ell^2</math>]].{{sfn|Helson|2010|p=24}} That is, if <math>\mu</math> places no mass on the sets of [[Lebesgue measure]] zero (i.e. <math>\mu_{pp}=0</math>), then <math>\hat{\mu}\to 0</math> as <math>|N| \to \infty</math>. Conversely, if <math>\hat{\mu}\to 0</math> as <math>|N| \to \infty</math>, then <math>\mu</math> places no mass on the [[countable set]]s. {{sfn|Lyons|1985|pp=155-156}}

A [[probability measure]] <math>\mu</math> on the circle is a Dirac mass [[if and only if]]
<math display="block">\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{1}{2N+1}\sum_{n=-N}^N|\widehat\mu(n)|^2=1.</math>
Here, the nontrivial implication follows from the fact that the weights <math>c_j</math> are positive and satisfy
<math display="block">1=\sum_j c_j^2\le\sum_j c_j\le 1,</math>
which forces <math>c_j^2=c_j</math> and thus <math>c_j=1</math>, so that there must be a single atom with mass <math>1</math>.

==Proof==
* First of all, we observe that if <math>\nu</math> is a [[complex measure]] on the circle then
:<math>\frac{1}{2N+1}\sum_{n=-N}^N\widehat{\nu}(n)=\int_{\mathbb T}f_N(z)\,d\nu(z),</math>
with <math>f_N(z)=\frac{1}{2N+1}\sum_{n=-N}^N z^{-n}</math>. The function <math>f_N</math> is bounded by <math>1</math> in [[absolute value]] and has <math>f_N(1)=1</math>, while <math>f_N(z)=\frac{z^{N+1}-z^{-N}}{(2N+1)(z-1)}</math> for <math>z\in\mathbb{T}\setminus\{1\}</math>, which converges to <math>0</math> as <math>N\to\infty</math>. Hence, by the [[dominated convergence theorem]],
:<math>\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{1}{2N+1}\sum_{n=-N}^N\widehat{\nu}(n)=\int_{\mathbb T}1_{\{1\}}(z)\,d\nu(z)=\nu(\{1\}).</math>
We now take <math>\mu'</math> to be the [[Pushforward measure|pushforward]] of <math>\overline\mu</math> under the inverse map on <math>\mathbb T</math>, namely <math>\mu'(B)=\overline{\mu(B^{-1})}</math> for any [[Borel set]] <math>B\subseteq\mathbb T</math>. This complex measure has Fourier coefficients <math>\widehat{\mu'}(n)=\overline{\widehat{\mu}(n)}</math>. We are going to apply the above to the [[convolution]] between <math>\mu</math> and <math>\mu'</math>, namely we choose <math>\nu=\mu*\mu'</math>, meaning that <math>\nu</math> is the [[Pushforward measure|pushforward]] of the measure <math>\mu\times\mu'</math> (on <math>\mathbb T\times\mathbb T</math>) under the product map <math>\cdot:\mathbb{T}\times\mathbb{T}\to\mathbb{T}</math>. By [[Fubini's theorem]]
:<math>\widehat{\nu}(n)=\int_{\mathbb{T}\times\mathbb{T}}(zw)^{-n}\,d(\mu\times\mu')(z,w)
=\int_{\mathbb T}\int_{\mathbb T}z^{-n}w^{-n}\,d\mu'(w)\,d\mu(z)=\widehat{\mu}(n)\widehat{\mu'}(n)=|\widehat{\mu}(n)|^2.</math>
So, by the identity derived earlier,
<math>\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{1}{2N+1}\sum_{n=-N}^N|\widehat{\mu}(n)|^2=\nu(\{1\})=\int_{\mathbb T\times\mathbb T}1_{\{zw=1\}}\,d(\mu\times\mu')(z,w).</math>
By [[Fubini's theorem]] again, the right-hand side equals
:<math>\int_{\mathbb T}\mu'(\{z^{-1}\})\,d\mu(z)=\int_{\mathbb T}\overline{\mu(\{z\})}\,d\mu(z)=\sum_j|\mu(\{z_j\})|^2=\sum_j|c_j|^2.</math>

* The proof of the analogous statement for the real line is identical, except that we use the identity
:<math>\frac{1}{2R}\int_{-R}^R\widehat\nu(\xi)\,d\xi=\int_{\mathbb R}f_R(x)\,d\nu(x)</math>
(which follows from [[Fubini's theorem]]), where <math>f_R(x)=\frac{1}{2R}\int_{-R}^R e^{-2\pi i\xi x}\,d\xi</math>.
We observe that <math>|f_R|\le 1</math>, <math>f_R(0)=1</math> and <math>f_R(x)=\frac{e^{2\pi iRx}-e^{-2\pi iRx}}{4\pi iRx}</math> for <math>x\neq 0</math>, which converges to <math>0</math> as <math>R\to\infty</math>. So, by [[Dominated convergence theorem|dominated convergence]], we have the analogous identity
:<math>\lim_{R\to\infty}\frac{1}{2R}\int_{-R}^R\widehat\nu(\xi)\,d\xi=\nu(\{0\}).</math>
